newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jobs before defence in French budget minefield.
newsitem.headline: Jobs before defence in French budget minefield.

text.p: French arms spending is under heavy fire as Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin struggles to draft a budget which delivers substantial new jobs next year without jeopardising France's qualification for European monetary union.

Jospin's team has limited room for manoeuvre in coupling an election pledge to create 350,000 new jobs while keeping the lid on state spending to cut the public deficit, hence the pressure on the defence ministry to cut investment.

In a country which has traditionally been a hefty military spender with big defence firms turning out Rafale fighter planes and Leclerc battle tanks, the cutbacks are highly sensitive even if small relative to the overall state budget mathematics.

As ministers digest the details of their letters from Jospin setting 1998 spending limits, finance ministry officials have reiterated employment and education are the main priorities -- and by implication, that defence must bear the brunt.

So far precise figures have not been released, but newspapers say the government could cut Defence Minister Alain Richard's budget for arms programmes by a two billion francs or more from an already reduced 1997 investment limit of 84.9 billion francs.

But even if arms spending cuts help fund plans to create up to 150,000 public sector jobs in 1998, as has been suggested, Jospin still has to find far bigger sums on the revenue side to cut the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as promised.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has stayed in Paris through the traditional August holiday period to help sort out the spending deliberations and now has to work out how to secure enough tax and non-fiscal income to hit the three percent target.
Although the spending leg has been completed, it is still not clear by just how much the two-month-old government will contain expenditure.

The general aim is to limit ministry operating costs as close as possible to the rate of inflation but the only message that has emerged from finance ministry sources is that the rise in the state budget increase will be considerably less than the rate of nominal GDP growth.

That, economists say, looks like an astute political move. If economic growth picks up the government will be able to say that it has kept the lid in spending in relative terms, without too much pain.

For the moment inflation is expected to come in at around 1.2 percent next year and the former centre-right government forecast 1998 GDP growth of 2.8 percent, which would give a nominal GDP rise of four percent.
Jospin is probably aiming to limit spending rises to around two percent, as government sources have recently suggested, economists say.

The next tricky part is the second leg of the budget -- how much the government can rely on economic growth to generate more tax income, and how much this is due to a windfall for export-led growth from the dollar's hefty rise against the franc.

The growth forecasts which the government comes up with in the coming weeks will also determine how much it will push for in "non-fiscal receipts", primarily transfers to the government from state-controlled companies.

The 1997 budget drawn up by former Prime Minister Alain Juppe included a transfer of 37 billion francs in pension liabilities from France Telecom, which strips 0.45 percentage points off the crucial public deficit figure.

Juppe's successors said in July an audit of public finances showed the 1997 public deficit was still heading for 3.5 to 3.7 percent of GDP and announced a 32-billion-franc package of corporate tax hikes and other savings to knock it down by 0.4 percentage points.

In 1998, depending on the growth forecast, the government may well need to carry out another funding tap of the France Telecom scale and one newspaper suggested on Tuesday it would seek 30 billion francs from state power utility Electricite de France.

Although the defence spending cuts look small by comparison, they have cast a cloud over the previous government's commitment in principle to order 48 Rafale fighter planes from Dassault Aviation between 1998 and 2002.

Sources close to the defence ministry said earlier this week that the Rafale programme was not in any case on the list of arms programmes slated for multi-annual purchasing commitments but that this did not mean the idea had been ruled out.
-- Brian Love, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
